subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What are the three states of matter?
back: The three states of matter are: • solid • liquid • gas

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define the kinetic theory of matter.
back: The kinetic theory of matter is a model that attempts to explain the properties of the three states of matter.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the particle arrangement in a solid?
back: The particle arrangement in a solid is: • a fixed pattern (lattice structure) • minimal space between particles

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Describe the arrangement of particles in a liquid.
back: The arrangement of particles in a liquid is: • closely packed • randomly arranged • free to flow past each other

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Solids have a fixed shape and volume.
back: True. Solids have a fixed shape and volume due to the fixed arrangement of their particles.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define the term compressibility in gases.
back: The term compressibility in gases refers to the ability of gases to be compressed due to the large spaces between the particles.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the definition of density in matter?
back: The definition of density in matter is the mass per unit volume of a substance, with solids generally having the highest density and gases the lowest.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the molecular arrangement in a gas.
back: The molecular arrangement in a gas is: • far apart • randomly arranged • moving freely in all directions

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which state of matter has the highest energy particles?
back: The state of matter that has the highest energy particles is a gas.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Describe the behaviour of a liquid in terms of its volume.
back: A liquid has: • a fixed volume • no fixed shape • takes the shape of its container

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Identify the particle arrangement that represents a solid.
back: The particles in a solid have a fixed structure in a lattice formation. This is the first diagram.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Identify the particle arrangement that represents a gas.
back: In a gas, the particles are spaced far apart and in a random arrangement. This is the third diagram.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Assuming all the particles have the same mass, which object has a greater density?
back: The object on the right is more dense because it has more mass per unit volume.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define density.
back: Density is the mass per unit volume of an object.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? A bucket filled with feathers will have a higher mass than the same bucket filled with sand.
back: False. A bucket filled with feathers will have a lower mass than the same bucket filled with sand because feathers have a lower density than sand.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the equation for density.
back: The equation for density is ρ = m/V Where: • ρ = density, measured in kilograms per metre cubed (kg m−3) • m = mass, measured in kilograms (kg) • V = volume, measured in metres cubed (m3)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What units are used for density if the mass is in grams and volume in cubic centimeters?
back: The units used for density if the mass is measured in grams and volume in cubic centimeters are grams per cubic centimetre (g cm<sup>−3</sup>).

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What units are used for density if mass is in kilograms and volume in cubic meters?
back: The units used for density if the mass is measured in kilograms and volume in cubic meters are kilograms per cubic metre (kg m<sup>−3</sup>).

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which is less dense: gases or liquids?
back: Gases are less dense than liquids because they tend to have more particles (and therefore more mass) per unit volume.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Convert 125 m to cm.
back: 125 m converted to cm is 12,500 cm • 125 × 100 = 12,500 cm

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How are cubic centimeters converted to cubic meters?
back: Cubic centimeters are converted to cubic meters by: • dividing by or • multiplying by 1 × 10−6 m3

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is absolute zero?
back: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, equal to 0 K or −273 °C.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define absolute zero.
back: Absolute zero is the temperature at which the molecules in a substance have zero kinetic energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? It is possible to have a temperature lower than 0 K.
back: False. It is not possible to have a temperature lower than 0 K.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How do you convert degrees Celsius to kelvin?
back: To convert degrees Celsius to kelvin, use the formula T = θ + 273 Where: • T = temperature, measured in kelvin (K) • θ = temperature, measured in degrees Celsius (°C)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How do you convert kelvin to degrees Celsius?
back: To convert kelvin to degrees Celsius, use the formula θ = T - 273 Where: • θ = temperature, measured in degrees Celsius (°C) • T = temperature, measured in kelvin (K)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does a temperature of 300 K correspond to in degrees Celsius?
back: A temperature of 300 K corresponds to 27 °C.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? A change in temperature of 1 K is equal to a change in temperature of 1 °C.
back: True. A change in temperature of 1 K is equal to a change in temperature of 1 °C.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the equation for the average kinetic energy of the particles in a gas.
back: The equation for the average kinetic energy of the particles in a gas is Ek = 3/2 kB T Where: Ek = kinetic energy, measured in joules (J); kB = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J K−1); T = absolute temperature, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Kinetic energy: \[ E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Absolute temperature is directly proportional to average kinetic energy.
back: True. Absolute temperature is directly proportional to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the value of the Boltzmann constant with its units.
back: Boltzmann constant, kB, is 1.38 × 10−23 J K−1

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define absolute temperature.
back: Absolute temperature is measured on the Kelvin scale, starting from absolute zero, where molecules have zero kinetic energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the relationship between temperature and kinetic energy?
back: The absolute temperature of a body is directly proportional to the average kinetic energy of the molecules within the body.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which formula connects the average speed of particles and the temperature of a gas?
back: The formula that connects the average speed of particles and temperature of a gas is v = √(3kB T/m) Where: v = average speed of gas particles, measured in meters per second (m s−1); kB = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J K−1); m = mass of particle, measured in kilograms (kg); T = absolute temperature, measured in kelvin (K)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define internal energy.
back:
Internal energy is defined as the sum of the total kinetic energy and the total intermolecular potential energy of the particles within a substance.

\[
U = KE + PE
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What happens to the internal energy of a substance when it gains thermal energy?
back: The internal energy of a substance increases when it gains thermal energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Temperature is a measure of the average potential energy of the molecules.
back: False. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the relationship between the thermal and kinetic energy of molecules?
back: The relationship between the thermal and kinetic energy of molecules is: • an increase in thermal energy leads to an increase in the average kinetic energy of molecules • this causes them to move at higher speeds

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How does potential energy change during the thermal expansion of a substance?
back: Potential energy increases during the thermal expansion of a substance as the particles get further away from each other.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the effect of a change in the potential energy of molecules on temperature?
back: There is no effect of a change in the potential energy of the molecules on the temperature.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How does the temperature of a substance change during a change of state?
back: The temperature of a substance does not change during a change of state.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What are the two energy types that make up internal energy?
back: The two energy types that make up internal energy are: • kinetic energy • potential energy

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which type of energy changes in a substance due to a change in temperature?
back: The type of energy that changes in a substance due to a change in temperature is kinetic energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Identify which gas in the diagram is being heated.
back: The gas on the right is being heated because it has higher kinetic energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the resultant temperature of both regions of the substance in the diagram.
back: The resultant temperature of both regions of the substance in the diagram is 50° C.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define thermal equilibrium.
back: Thermal equilibrium is when two substances in contact with each other no longer exchange heat energy as they both reach an equal temperature.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Thermal energy is always transferred from a colder region to a hotter region.
back: False. Thermal energy is always transferred from a hotter region to a cooler region.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What happens to the temperatures of two regions in thermal contact?
back: The temperatures of two regions in thermal contact will change as follows: • the hotter region will cool down • the cooler region will heat up • until they reach the same temperature

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does thermal equilibrium mean in terms of energy transfer between two regions?
back: Thermal equilibrium means there is no longer thermal energy transfer between the two regions.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is required for two regions to reach thermal equilibrium?
back: For two regions to reach thermal equilibrium they need to be in thermal contact.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the direction of energy flow when ice is placed in room temperature water.
back: The direction of thermal energy flow when ice is placed in room temperature water is from the water to the ice.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What determines the final temperature in thermal equilibrium between water and ice?
back: The final temperature in the thermal equilibrium between water and ice depends on the initial temperature difference between the water and the ice.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which direction does thermal energy flow when two regions are at different temperatures?
back: When two regions are at different temperatures, energy flows from the hotter to the cooler region.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State how the internal energy changes from the bottom of the diagram to the top.
back: From the bottom of the diagram to the top the internal energy increases because the particles in the gas have more kinetic energy than in a solid.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is a change of state?
back: A change of state is when matter changes from one phase (solid, liquid, or gas) into another.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define melting.
back: Melting is when a substance changes from a solid to a liquid as it absorbs thermal energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is freezing?
back: Freezing is when a substance changes from a liquid to a solid as it releases thermal energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does vaporisation mean?
back: Vaporisation is when a substance changes from a liquid to a gas as it absorbs thermal energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define condensation.
back: Condensation is when a substance changes from a gas to a liquid as it releases thermal energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How does thermal energy affect the molecules during a phase change?
back: Thermal energy affects the potential energy, so the spacing between the molecules changes during a phase change.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which phase changes occur at the boiling point of a substance?
back: At the boiling point of a substance, vaporisation and condensation occur.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the boiling and freezing points of water.
back: The boiling point of water is 100 °C and the freezing point is 0 °C.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What happens when thermal energy is released from water vapour at 100 °C?
back: When thermal energy is released from water vapour at 100 °C, it condenses back into liquid water.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define specific heat capacity.
back:
Specific heat capacity is the amount of energy required to change the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (or 1°C).

Useful formula — Specific heat capacity:
\[
Q = mc\Delta T
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the equation for the thermal energy transferred, Q, to a substance?
back: The equation for thermal energy transferred, Q, to a substance is Q = mcΔT. Where: m = mass of substance, measured in kilograms (kg); c = specific heat capacity of substance, measured in joules per kilogram per kelvin (J kg−1 K−1); ΔT = change in temperature, measured in kelvin (K) or degrees Celsius (°)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? The higher the specific heat capacity of a substance, the faster it heats up or cools down.
back: False. The higher the specific heat capacity of a substance, the longer it takes to warm up or cool down. Useful formula — Specific heat capacity: \[ Q = mc\Delta T \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does c represent in the equation Q = mcΔT?
back: c represents the specific heat capacity of a substance measured in J kg−1 K−1.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How does the mass of an object affect the thermal energy needed to change its temperature?
back: The greater the mass of an object, the more thermal energy needed to change its temperature.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which phase changes require thermal energy to be absorbed by a substance?
back: The phase changes that require thermal energy to be absorbed by a substance are melting and vaporisation.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the definition of ΔT in relation to specific heat capacity?
back: ΔT is the change in temperature in kelvin or degrees Celsius (K or °C). Useful formula — Specific heat capacity: \[ Q = mc\Delta T \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does the specific heat capacity indicate about a substance?
back:
The specific heat capacity indicates how much energy is required to change the temperature of a substance.

Useful formula — Specific heat capacity:
\[
Q = mc\Delta T
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: The diagram shows the heating of ice and then water with a Bunsen burner. State the temperature of the water as it is melted.
back: The temperature of the water as it is melted is 0° C.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define specific latent heat.
back:
Specific latent heat is defined as the amount of energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.

Useful formula — Specific latent heat:
\[
Q = mL
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the equation for thermal energy transferred in terms of specific latent heat, L.
back: The equation for thermal energy transferred in terms of specific latent heat is Q = mL Where: Q = thermal energy transferred, measured in joules (J); m = mass of substance, measured in kilograms (kg); L = specific latent heat, measured in joules per kilogram (J kg−1) Useful formula — Specific latent heat: \[ Q = mL \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does L represent in the equation Q = mL?
back: L represents the specific latent heat of a substance in J kg−1.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How is the specific latent heat of fusion defined?
back:
The specific latent heat of fusion is defined as the energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid (or vice versa) at constant temperature.

Useful formula — Specific latent heat:
\[
Q = mL
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does the specific latent heat of vaporisation describe?
back:
The specific latent heat of vaporisation describes the energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas (or vice versa) at constant temperature.

Useful formula — Specific latent heat:
\[
Q = mL
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which is higher: the specific latent heat of vaporisation or fusion?
back:
The specific latent heat of vaporisation is always higher than the specific latent heat of fusion for a given substance.

This is because vaporisation separates particles much further apart into a gas, so more energy is needed to overcome intermolecular attractions than during fusion, where particles only move from solid positions into a liquid.

Useful formula — Specific latent heat:
\[
Q = mL
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What happens to the intermolecular forces of a substance during vaporisation?
back: The intermolecular forces of a substance during vaporisation need to be completely overcome.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define specific latent heat of fusion, Lf.
back: The specific latent heat of fusion, Lf, is the energy absorbed when 1 kg of solid melts to become liquid at a constant temperature or the energy released when 1 kg of liquid freezes to become solid at a constant temperature. Useful formula — Specific latent heat: \[ Q = mL \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the temperature gradient equation in terms of heat flow?
back: The temperature gradient equation in terms of heat flow is ΔQ/Δt = kA(ΔT/Δx) Where: ΔQ/Δt = flow of thermal energy per second, measured in watts (W); k = thermal conductivity of the material, measured in watts per metre per kelvin (W m−1 K−1); ΔT = temperature difference, measured in kelvin (K) or degrees Celsius (° C); Δx = thickness of material, measured in metres (m)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Metals are the best thermal conductors.
back: True. Metals are the best thermal conductors because they have a high number of free electrons.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How is thermal energy transferred in conduction?
back: Thermal energy is transferred in conduction through atomic vibrations.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the main mechanism of thermal energy transfer in solids?
back: The main mechanism of thermal energy transfer in solids is conduction.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which of the following materials has the highest thermal conductivity air, rubber, or copper?
back: Copper has the highest thermal conductivity among air, rubber, and copper.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define the term free electron collision in conduction.
back: Free electron collision is a mechanism in conduction where free electrons in metals collide with atoms, transferring energy.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the role of delocalised electrons in thermal conduction in metals?
back: Delocalised electrons increase the rate of energy transfer in thermal conduction in metals, making metals good thermal conductors.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Draw an arrow to show the direction of the movement of the air particles due to the heat from the fire.
back: The air moves vertically upward above the fire as the hot gas expands and becomes less dense.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Draw an arrow to show the direction of the movement of the cooler, denser air in the convection current.
back: The cooler, denser air moves vertically downward away from the heat of the fire.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the main way that energy is transferred through gases and liquids?
back: Convection is the main way that heat travels through liquids and gases.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define thermal convection.
back: Thermal convection is the transfer of thermal energy through the movement of a fluid due to variations in density.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define a convection current.
back: A convection current is the motion that results when hot fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks, creating a circular flow.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Convection can occur in solids.
back: False. Convection cannot occur in solids because the particles are unable to travel relative to one another.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What happens to the density of a fluid when it is heated?
back: The density of a fluid decreases when it is heated because the fluid expands.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How is thermal energy transferred during convection?
back: Thermal energy is transferred during convection by the movement of groups of atoms or molecules in a fluid as a result of variations in density.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which states of matter does convection occur in?
back: Convection occurs in liquids and gases.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is an example of convection in nature?
back: Examples of convection in nature are: atmospheric convection (which leads to winds and sea breezes); thunderheads (clouds that appear before a storm); convection currents in the Earth's mantle (leading to continental drift); ocean currents; solar convections (leading to sunspots and solar flares)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Describe what happens in a beaker of water with potassium permanganate during convection.
back: In a beaker of water with potassium permanganate, the heated water rises, carrying the dissolved purple crystal, while cooler water sinks, forming a convection current.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What causes convection currents in the Earth's mantle?
back: Convection currents in the Earth's mantle are caused by the movement of heated and cooled material, leading to continental drift.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is thermal radiation?
back: Thermal radiation is heat transfer by means of electromagnetic radiation, usually in the infrared region.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Thermal radiation requires matter to propagate.
back: False. Thermal radiation does not require matter to propagate and can travel through a vacuum.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define black-body radiation.
back: Black-body radiation is the thermal radiation emitted by all bodies, which can be in the form of infrared light, visible light, or other wavelengths depending on the temperature.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is a perfect black body?
back:
A perfect black body is an object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it and does not reflect or transmit any.

Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law:
\[
P = \sigma A T^4
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How does the surface colour of an object affect thermal radiation?
back: The surface colour of an object affects thermal radiation because: • dark, dull objects are better at emitting and absorbing radiation • light, shiny objects are worse at emitting and absorbing radiation

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What happens to the thermal radiation of an object as its temperature increases?
back: The thermal radiation of an object increases as its temperature increases.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which type of electromagnetic waves are most commonly emitted as thermal radiation?
back: The electromagnetic waves that are most commonly emitted as thermal radiation are infrared.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the relationship between temperature and the peak wavelength of emitted radiation?
back: The relationship between temperature and the peak wavelength of emitted radiation is they are inversely proportional. Useful formula — Wien’s law: \[ \lambda_{\max}T = b \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How does a meteorite dissipate thermal energy on the Moon?
back: A meteorite dissipates thermal energy on the Moon via conduction (to the Moon's surface) and radiation (infrared photons travelling through the vacuum of space).

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the factors affecting the amount of thermal radiation emitted by an object.
back: The factors affecting the amount of thermal radiation emitted by an object are: • surface colour • texture • surface area

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is apparent brightness?
back: Apparent brightness is the intensity of radiation received on Earth from a star.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define luminosity.
back:
Luminosity is the total power output of radiation emitted by a star.

Useful formula — Luminosity:
\[
L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What unit is apparent brightness measured in?
back: Apparent brightness is measured in watts per metre squared (W m<sup>−2</sup>).

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What unit is luminosity measured in?
back:
Luminosity is measured in units of watts (W).

Useful formula — Luminosity:
\[
L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? Luminosity and apparent brightness are the same.
back: False. The luminosity is the total power output of the star, whereas the apparent brightness is what is measured by an observer on Earth. Useful formula — Luminosity: \[ L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the inverse square law of radiation.
back: The inverse square law of radiation is b = L/(4πd2) Where: b = apparent brightness of light observed on Earth, measured in watts per metre squared (W m−2); L = luminosity of light source, measured in watts (W); d = distance between star and Earth, measured in metres (m)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How is the apparent brightness of a star related to the distance to the observer?
back: The apparent brightness of a star decreases with the square of the distance to the observer.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which factors determine the apparent brightness of a star?
back: The factors that determine the apparent brightness of a star are: • the luminosity of the star • the distance to the observer

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What happens to the intensity of light when the distance to the observer is doubled?
back:
The intensity of light is reduced to one-fourth when the distance to the observer is doubled.

Useful formula — Intensity from luminosity:
\[
I = \frac{L}{4\pi r^2}
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define the Stefan-Boltzmann Law.
back:
The Stefan-Boltzmann Law states that the total energy emitted by a black body per unit area per second is proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature of the body.

Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law:
\[
P = \sigma A T^4
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does the Stefan-Boltzmann Law calculate?
back:
The Stefan-Boltzmann Law calculates the total power radiated by a perfect black body based on its temperature and surface area.

Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law:
\[
P = \sigma A T^4
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the equation for the Stefan-Boltzmann Law.
back: The equation for the Stefan-Boltzmann law is P = σAT4 Where: P = total power emitted across all wavelengths, measured in watts (W); σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant; A = surface area of body, measured in metres squared (m2); T = absolute temperature of a body, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law: \[ P = \sigma A T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, σ?
back: The Stefan-Boltzmann constant, σ, is a physical constant equal to 5.67 × 10−8 W m−2 K−4. Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law: \[ P = \sigma A T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the formula to calculate the luminosity of a star using the Stefan-Boltzmann Law?
back: The formula for the Stefan-Boltzmann law is L = 4πr2σT4 Where: L = luminosity of the star, measured in watts (W); r = radius of star, measured in metres (m); σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant; T = absolute temperature of a body, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Luminosity: \[ L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the relationship between the temperature and power emitted by a black body?
back: The relationship between the temperature and power emitted by a black body is that power is directly proportional to temperature to the power of four. Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law: \[ P = \sigma A T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the surface area formula for a spherical object?
back: The surface area formula of a spherical object is A = 4πr2 Where: • r = radius of the sphere, measured in metres (m)

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? The Stefan-Boltzmann Law can be used to calculate the luminosity of celestial objects.
back: True. The Stefan-Boltzmann Law is often used to calculate the luminosity of celestial objects, such as stars. Useful formula — Luminosity: \[ L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What factors determine the total power radiated by a black body?
back:
The factors that determine the total power radiated by a black body are absolute temperature and surface area.

Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law:
\[
P = \sigma A T^4
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Which equation is used to find the radius of a star if its luminosity and temperature are known?
back: The equation is used to find the radius of a star if its luminosity and temperature are known is r = √(L/(4πσT4)) Where: r = radius of star, measured in metres (m); L = luminosity of the star, measured in watts (W); σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant; T = absolute temperature of a body, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Luminosity: \[ L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does Wien’s displacement law state?
back:
Wien’s displacement law states that the black body radiation curve for different temperatures peaks at a wavelength that is inversely proportional to the temperature.

Useful formula — Wien’s law:
\[
\lambda_{\max}T = b
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define the quantity λmax in Wien’s displacement law.
back: The quantity λmax in Wien's displacement law is the wavelength at which radiation is emitted at the greatest intensity. Useful formula — Wien’s law: \[ \lambda_{\max}T = b \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: State the equation for Wien’s displacement law.
back: The equation for Wien’s displacement law is λmax T = 2.9 × 10−3 m K Where: • T = surface temperature of an object, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Wien’s law: \[ \lambda_{\max}T = b \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: True or False? The peak wavelength of a black body decreases as temperature increases.
back: True. The peak wavelength of a black body decreases as temperature increases. Useful formula — Wien’s law: \[ \lambda_{\max}T = b \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What does Wien’s displacement law indicate about an object's temperature and wavelength at its peak intensity?
back:
Wien’s displacement law indicates that the higher the temperature of an object, the shorter the wavelength at the peak intensity.

Useful formula — Wien’s law:
\[
\lambda_{\max}T = b
\]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: How does the radiation intensity change as an object heats up?
back: The radiation intensity increases for every wavelength as an object heats up.

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: Define the quantity T in the equation for Wien’s displacement law.
back: The quantity T in the equation for Wien’s displacement law is the surface temperature of an object in kelvin (K). Useful formula — Wien’s law: \[ \lambda_{\max}T = b \]

subtopicFull: B.1 Thermal Energy Transfers: Temperature, specific heat capacity, phase changes.
front: What is the relationship between wavelength and temperature in Wien’s displacement law?
back: The relationship between wavelength and temperature in Wien’s displacement law is inverse proportionality. Useful formula — Wien’s law: \[ \lambda_{\max}T = b \]

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Define emissivity.
back: Emissivity is the ratio of the power radiated per unit area by an object compared to that of an ideal black body at the same temperature.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: State the equation for emissivity.
back: The equation for emissivity is e = power radiated by object / power radiated by a black body

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: What assumptions do emissivity calculations make?
back: Emissivity calculations make the following assumptions: • the black body is at the same temperature as the object • the black body has the same dimensions as the object

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: What is the emissivity value for a perfect black body?
back: The emissivity value for a perfect black body is 1. Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law: \[ P = \varepsilon \sigma A T^4 \] For a perfect black body, \(\varepsilon = 1\).

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: State the Stefan-Boltzmann law equation for an object which is not a black body.
back: The Stefan-Boltzmann law for an object that is not a black body is P = eσAT4 Where: P = total power emitted by object, measured in watts (W); e = emissivity of object (no units); σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant; A = total surface area of the object / black body (these are assumed to be the same), measured in metres squared (m2); T = absolute temperature of the object / black body (these are assumed to be the same), measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law: \[ P = \sigma A T^4 \]

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Define albedo.
back: Albedo is the ratio of the total scattered power to the total incident power of radiation on a surface.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: State the equation for albedo.
back: The equation for albedo is a = total scattered power / total incident power

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: State one factor that affectsss the albedo of Earth.
back: The three factors that affect the albedo of Earth are: cloud formations due to seasons and day; latitude; terrain; incident angle on the surface of the Earth

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: The Earth has an albedo of 0.3. What does that represent?
back: An albedo of 0.3 means that 30% of the radiation from the Sun that reaches the Earth's surface is reflected back into the atmosphere.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: What does an albedo of 1 represent?
back: An albedo of 1 will represent a surface which scatters all incident radiation.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Define the solar constant.
back: The solar constant is the intensity of the Sun's radiation arriving perpendicularly on the Earth's atmosphere when the Earth is at its mean distance from the Sun.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Give one reason why the solar constant varies throughout the year.
back: Reasons why the solar constant varies throughout the year are: • the elliptical orbit of the Earth means that Earth differs in its distance from the Sun • the Sun's output varies during its sunspot cycle

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: What assumptions do solar constant calculations make?
back: Solar constant calculations make the following assumptions: • solar radiation is incident on a plane perpendicular to the Earth's surface • the Earth is at a mean distance from the Sun

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? Different planets have different solar constants.
back: True. Different planets have different solar constants because they are different distances away from the Sun.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: What is the mean value of the radiative power or intensity?
back: The mean value of the radiative power or intensity is S/4 • S × (πr2 / 4πr2) = S/4

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: What are the main greenhouse gases?
back: The main greenhouse gases are: water vapour (H<sub>2</sub>O); carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>); methane (CH<sub>4</sub>); nitrous oxide (N<sub>2</sub>O)

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Which of the main greenhouse gases is most abundant in the atmosphere?
back: The greenhouse gas that is most abundant in the atmosphere is water vapour.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: What is a greenhouse gas?
back: A greenhouse gas is a gas that absorbs re-radiated radiation, trapping the radiation in the Earth's atmosphere.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Which greenhouse gases contribute the most to the greenhouse effect?
back: The greenhouse gases that contribute most to the greenhouse effect are: • carbon dioxide (CO2) • water vapour (H2O)

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? Ozone absorbs almost 100% of incoming UV radiation.
back: True. Ozone absorbs almost 100% of incoming UV radiation. Ozone also absorbs outgoing infrared radiation.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation.
back: True. Carbon dioxide strongly absorbs infrared radiation at 15μm.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? Water vapour absorbs infrared radiation.
back: True. Water vapour absorbs infrared radiation.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? Increasing concentrations of ozone in the atmosphere are significantly contributing to the greenhouse effect.
back: False. Increasing concentrations of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere are significantly contributing to the greenhouse effect. The concentration of ozone in the atmosphere is too low to significantly contribute to the greenhouse effect.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? Most of the radiation reaching Earth from the Sun is ultraviolet and visible light.
back: True. Most of the radiation reaching Earth from the Sun is ultraviolet and visible light.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? Visible light is absorbed by the atmosphere.
back: False. Visible light is not absorbed by the atmosphere; it is absorbed by the Earth's surface. At night, the Earth re-radiates this energy as infrared radiation.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Describe the process of global warming using the resonance model.
back: The process of global warming using the resonance model is as follows: visible light is absorbed by the Earth's surface in the day; the energy is re-radiated as infrared during the night; some of the infrared is reflected out to space; some of the infrared is absorbed by greenhouse gases; greenhouse gases reflect the infrared back to Earth; heat energy becomes trapped inside the Earth's atmosphere

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? According to the molecular energy level model, high-frequency UV light causes atoms to vibrate.
back: False. High-frequency UV light breaks molecular bonds. It is infrared radiation that causes atoms to vibrate.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? According to the molecular energy level model, greenhouse gases have a natural frequency close to that of infrared, so when they absorb infrared radiation, they resonate, causing the molecules to heat up.
back: True. According to the molecular energy level model, greenhouse gases have a natural frequency close to that of infrared, so when they absorb infrared radiation, they resonate, causing the molecules to heat up.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Give one example of human activity that has led to an increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
back: Examples of human activity that have led to an increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere are: • burning fossil fuels • burning wood • deforestation

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Give one example of human activity that has led to an increase in methane in the atmosphere.
back: Examples of human activity that have led to an increase in methane in the atmosphere are: • decay of organic matter • farming

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: Give one example of human activity that has led to an increase in nitrous oxide in the atmosphere.
back: Examples of human activity that have led to an increase in nitrous oxide in the atmosphere are: • artificial fertilisers • burning fossil fuels

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: True or False? If the Earth's incoming and outgoing energy is balanced, then the temperature of the Earth will rise.
back: False. If the Earth's incoming and outgoing energy is balanced, then the temperature of the Earth will remain constant.

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: For the Earth's temperature to remain constant, what would the value of incident radiation need to be?
back: For the Earth's temperature to remain constant, the incident radiation would need to be 290 W m−2. • incident intensity = 140 + 150

subtopicFull: B.2 Greenhouse Effect: Radiation, energy balance of the Earth.
front: In the scenario shown in this energy balance diagram, explain whether the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere increases, decreases or stays the same.
back: In the scenario shown in this energy balance diagram, the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere increases because the incident intensity is greater than the outgoing intensity.

subtopicFull: B.3 – Gas Laws
front: For a fixed volume of gas at a constant temperature , increasing the number of gas particles will [...] the pressure .
back:
From the ideal gas equation,

\[
PV = nRT
\]

if the volume \(V\) and temperature \(T\) are fixed, then pressure \(P\) is directly proportional to the amount of gas \(n\).

So increasing the number of gas particles increases \(n\), which increases \(P\).

subtopicFull: B.3 – Gas Laws
front: The internal energy of an ideal gas is determined only by the [...] energy of its particles.
back:
The internal energy of an ideal gas is determined only by the kinetic energy of its particles.

There are no intermolecular forces of attraction, so there is no potential energy .

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Define pressure.
back: Pressure is the force applied per unit area.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? When an object is immersed in a fluid, forces act parallel to its surfaces to produce pressure.
back: False. When an object is immersed in a fluid, forces act perpendicular to its surfaces to produce pressure.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: How do gas particles exert a force on the walls of a container?
back: Gas particles exert a force on the container by colliding with the walls. Over the area of a wall, this exerts a pressure.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Which person exerts a higher pressure on the ground, a 70 kg person standing on one foot or a 100 kg person standing on both feet? Assume their feet are the same size.
back: The 70 kg person on one foot exerts a higher pressure. The 70 kg person exerts ~700 N per foot but the 100 kg person exerts ~500 N per foot, so the 70 kg person exerts a greater pressure.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Recall the equation for pressure.
back: The equation for pressure is P = F/A Where: • P = pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • F = force, measured in newtons (N) • A = area measured in metres squared (m^2)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? Gas particles travelling at a greater speed exert a greater force on container walls.
back: True. When gas particles collide with container walls at higher speeds, they exert a greater force and hence a greater pressure on the container.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? The frequency of collisions between particles and container walls is increased, but their speed remains constant. The pressure exerted by the gas is unchanged.
back: False. When gas particles collide with container walls more frequently, the average force is increased so the pressure increases.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Define one mole.
back: One mole is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary entities as the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: How many atoms are in one mole of argon (Ar)? Argon is a monatomic gas.
back: In one mole of argon there are \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) atoms - this is the Avogadro constant.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? There are 6.02 × 10^23 atoms in one mole of gaseous carbon dioxide.
back: False. In one mole of there are 6.02 × 10^23 elementary elements, but each elementary element has three atoms so there are 1.86 × 10^24 atoms in one mole of .

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Write the equation for the number of moles in a substance when the number of particles is known.
back: The equation for the number of moles is n = N/N_A Where: • n = number of moles (mol) • N= number of particles (particles may be atoms or molecules, depending on the substance) • N_A= Avogadro constant, measured in particles per mole (mol^−1)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Write the equation for molar mass when number of moles and mass is known.
back: The equation for molar mass is m_r = m/n Where: • m_r= molar mass, measured in grams per mole (g mol^−1) • m= mass of substance, measured in grams (g) • n= number of moles (mol)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? There are fewer atoms in one mole of than there are in one mole of .
back: True. While both contain the same number of molecules, there are more atoms in a molecule of than in a molecule of .

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: How would the molar mass of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) be determined if the relative atom masses of H and O are known?
back:
The molar mass in \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the molecule.

For \(\mathrm{H_2O}\):

\[
M = 2A_r(\mathrm{H}) + A_r(\mathrm{O})
\]

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What relation does an ideal gas obey?
back: An ideal gas obeys the relation PV ∝ T or PV/T = constant Where: • P = pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • V = volume, measured in cubic metres \(\mathrm{m^3}\) • T = temperature, measured in kelvin (K)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Define the meaning of an empirical law.
back: An empirical law is formed based on observed data from experiments, rather than being derived from theory.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Write the equation for Boyle's law in terms of initial and final states.
back: Boyle's law in terms of initial and final states is P1V1 = P2V2 for a constant temperature. Where: • P_1 = initial pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • P_2 = final pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • V_1 = is initial volume, measured in cubic metres (m3) • V_2 = final volume, measured in cubic metres (m3)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What is the relationship shown by the graph below?
back: The graph shows that pressure is inversely proportional to volume.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Write the equation for Charles' law in terms of initial and final states.
back: Charles' law in terms of initial and final states is V1/T1 = V2/T2 for a constant pressure. Where: • T_1 = initial temperature, measured in kelvin (K) • T_2 = final temperature, measured in kelvin (K) • V_1 = initial volume, measured in cubic metres (m3) • V_2 = final volume, measured in cubic metres (m3)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? The graph showing Charles' law is curved. The axes are volume and temperature (K).
back: False. The graph representing Charles' law is a straight line passing through the origin. The axes are volume and temperature (K).

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Write the equation for Gay-Lussac's law in terms of initial and final states.
back: Charles' law in terms of initial and final states is P1/T1 = P2/T2 for a constant volume. Where: • T_1 = initial temperature, measured in kelvin (K) • T_2 = final temperature, measured in kelvin (K) • P_1 = initial pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • P_2 = final pressure , measured in pascals (Pa)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? The graph below shows a directly proportional relationship.
back: False. Gay-Lussac's law states that pressure is directly proportional to temperature in kelvin. This graph shows temperature in degrees Celsius and does not pass through the origin, so is not directly proportional.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Write the ideal gas equation when the number of moles is known.
back: The ideal gas equation for a known number of moles is PV = nRT Where: • P = pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • V = volume, measured in metres cubed (m^3) • n = number of moles measured in moles (mol) • R = gas constant, measured in joules per kelvin per mole (J K^−1 mol^−1) • T = temperature, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Ideal gas equation: \[ PV = nRT = Nk_B T \]

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Write the ideal gas equation when the number of particles is known.
back: The ideal gas equation for a known number of moles is PV = Nk_BT Where: • P = pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • V = volume, measured in metres-cubed (m^3) • N = number of particles • k_B = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J K^−1) • T = temperature, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Ideal gas equation: \[ PV = nRT = Nk_B T \]

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? The ideal gas law equation can be derived from the empirical gas laws for constant pressure and constant volume.
back: False. The ideal gas law equation can be derived from the empirical gas laws for constant pressure, constant volume and constant temperature. Useful formula — Ideal gas equation: \[ PV = nRT = Nk_B T \]

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: How are the Boltzmann constant, gas constant and Avogadro constant related?
back: The Boltzmann constant, gas constant and Avogadro constant are related by: \[ k_{B} = \frac{R}{N_{A}} \] Equivalently: \[ R = N_{A}k_{B} \] Where: • \(k_{B}\) = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J K−1) • \(R\) = molar gas constant, measured in joules per kelvin per mole (J K−1 mol−1) • \(N_{A}\) = Avogadro constant, measured in particles per mole (mol−1)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What is the ideal gas equation for a known number of particles when temperature is the subject?
back: The ideal gas equation for a known number of particles with temperature as the subject is T = PV/(Nk_B) Where: • P = pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • V = volume, measured in metres-cubed (m^3) • N = number of particles • k_B = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J K^−1) • T = temperature, measured in kelvin (K) Useful formula — Ideal gas equation: \[ PV = nRT = Nk_B T \]

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: How can the motion of particles in a gas be described?
back: Particles in a gas move: • randomly • at high speeds

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What two properties of gases does the kinetic theory of gases connect?
back: The kinetic theory of gases connects: • the microscopic properties of particles, e.g. mass and speed • the macroscopic properties of particles, e.g. pressure and volume

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? Kinetic theory assumes that there is a small gravitational force between particles.
back: False. Kinetic theory assumes that no forces act between particles other than when they collide.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What are three assumptions made about forces in kinetic theory?
back: Any three of the following assumptions about forces made in kinetic theory: • The molecules obey Newton's laws of motion • There are no forces between the molecules except during collisions • External forces (e.g. gravity) are ignored • Each particle exerts a force on the wall of the container with which it collides.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What are three assumptions about the quantity and size of molecules in kinetic theory?
back: Any three of the following assumptions about molecules in kinetic theory: • A gas consists of identical molecules in a container • Molecules have negligible volume and are point particles • The number of molecules of gas in a container is very large so the average behaviour is considered

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What are three assumptions made about collisions in kinetic theory?
back: Three of the following assumptions about collisions in kinetic theory: • The molecules collide elastically • There are no forces between the molecules except during collisions • The time of a collision between molecules is negligible compared to the time between collisions • Each particle exerts a force on the wall of the container with which it collides.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? Real gases obey the ideal gas law.
back: False. Real gases do not obey the ideal gas law as the assumptions of kinetic theory are not always valid. Useful formula — Ideal gas equation: \[ PV = nRT = Nk_B T \]

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: What are the conditions for a gas to be considered an ideal gas?
back: The conditions for a gas to be ideal are: • the gas pressure is low • the gas density is low • the temperature is sufficiently higher than the boiling point of the substance

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Show that the change in momentum for a particle of mass, m, and initial speed, +v, is −2mv when it collides with a container wall.
back: The change in momentum is Δp = mΔv = m(v_f − v_i) After rebounding elastically, speed is −v in the negative direction. Therefore, change in momentum is Δp = mΔv = m((−v) − v) = −2mv

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Show that, for a particle with speed, v, crossing a container of width, L, the time between collisions with a particular wall is 2L/v.
back: To find the time between collisions: • The time between collisions is given by Δt = distance/speed • Between collisions, the particle travels the width of the container and back, 2L • The speed is v so Δt = 2L/v

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? If the time between collisions with a container wall for a particle is 2L/v and the change in momentum is −2mv then the force on the container wall is −mv2/L.
back: False. Force is rate of change of momentum, so −2mv/(2L/v) = −mv2/L is the force on the particle. The particle exerts an equal and opposite force of +mv2/L on the wall.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: State the kinetic theory of gases equation.
back: The kinetic theory of gases equation is P = ⅓ρv2 Where: • P = pressure, measured in pascals (Pa) • ρ = density of the gas, measured in kilograms per metre-cubed (kg ) • v = average speed of particles, measured in metres per second (m )

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? When a single gas particle is assumed to travel only in the x direction, the square of its speed is only one third of the particle's actual speed in three dimensions.
back: True. The squared speed in the x direction, only accounts, on average, for one third of the square of the overall speed if the particle moves in all directions, so = ⅓v2

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: State the kinetic energy equation.
back: The kinetic energy equation is = ½mv2 Where: • = kinetic energy, measured in joules (J) • m = mass, measured in kilograms (kg) • v = speed, measured in metres per second (m) Useful formula — Kinetic energy: \[ E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \]

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: How are the following three equations combined to give E_k = 3/2 T? • P = Nmv2/(3V) • PV = NT • = ½mv2
back: To obtain the equation = 3/2 T: • Combine equations 1 and 3: P = Nmv2/(3V) = N × 2/(3V) • Rearrange this and equate to equation 2: 2/3 N = PV and PV = NT • 2/3 N = NT • Rearrange to give: = 3/2T

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: In terms of the Boltzmann constant, what is the total internal energy of N particles of an ideal gas?
back: Total internal energy of an ideal gas is U = 3/2 NT Where: • U = total internal energy, measured in joules (J) • N = number of ideal gas particles • = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J ) • T = temperature, measured in kelvin (K)

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: True or False? Total internal energy and total kinetic energy are not equal for a real gas.
back: True. In an ideal gas, total internal energy is total kinetic energy. In a real gas, however, internal energy is the sum of all kinetic and potential energies which arise from intermolecular interactions.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front: Why is it not possible to state that internal energy is proportional to temperature for  gas?
back: This relationship only applies to monatomic gases. is diatomic so also has rotational kinetic energy.

subtopicFull: B.3 Gas Laws: Moles, ideal gases, Boltzmann equation.
front:
A low pressure sample of monatomic helium gas has an initial temperature of 450 K and a final temperature of 1800 K.
By what factor has its internal energy increased?
back: For an ideal gas, internal energy is proportional to temperature. Temperature has increased by a factor of 4 so the internal energy has also increased by a factor of 4.

subtopicFull: B.4 – Thermodynamics
front: A heat engine operates with a hot reservoir at 90°C and a cold reservoir at 25°C. During a cycle, it absorbs 940J of energy from the hot reservoir and returns 560J to the cold reservoir. Calculate the change in entropy during one complete cycle.
back:
We must extrapolate the given formula for change in entropy:
\[\Delta{S} = \frac{\Delta{Q}}{T} = \frac{Q_\text{in}}{T_\text{h}} - \frac{Q_\text{out}}{T_\text{c}}\]
\[\Delta{S} = \frac{+940}{90 + 273} - \frac{560}{25 + 273}\]

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Why do ideal gases have no potential energy?
back: Ideal gases have no potential energy because there are no intermolecular forces in an ideal gas.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: What is the relationship between kinetic energy and internal energy for an ideal gas?
back: For an ideal gas, internal energy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: True or False? As the internal energy of an ideal gas increases, the average speed of the particles increases.
back: True. Internal energy is directly proportional to temperature, which is directly proportional to kinetic energy. As kinetic energy increases, so does the average speed of particles.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: State the equation for the first law of thermodynamics.
back:
The first law of thermodynamics can be written as:

\[
Q = \Delta U + W
\]

where \(Q\) is the thermal energy supplied to the system, \(\Delta U\) is the change in internal energy, and \(W\) is the work done by the system.

This means energy supplied by heating either increases the internal energy of the system or is used to do work.

If \(W_{\mathrm{on}}\) means work done on the system, then:

\[
\Delta U = Q + W_{\mathrm{on}}
\]

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: What is the sign of W when work is done on a gas?
back: When work is done on a gas, W is negative. Useful formula — Work done: \[ W = Fs\cos\theta \]

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: What is the sign of W when work is done by a gas?
back: When work is done by a gas, W is positive. Useful formula — Work done: \[ W = Fs\cos\theta \]

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: What is the sign of ΔU when a gas is heated and work is done on a gas?
back: When a gas is heated and work is done to it, its internal energy increases so ΔU is positive. Useful formula — Work done: \[ W = Fs\cos\theta \]

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: What is the sign of ΔU when a gas transfers heat to its surroundings and expands?
back: When a gas transfers heat away, Q is negative and when it expands it does work so Wis negative. This means its internal energy decreases so ΔU is negative.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.

back: Using the first law of thermodynamics:

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: True or False? If a gas is heated, it must expand.
back: False. From the first law of thermodynamics, If a gas is heated, Q is positive, but the energy may increase the system's internal energy instead of causing expansion. So W can be zero while the first law is still obeyed.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Define the entropy of a system.
back: The entropy of a system is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of the particles and their energies, i.e. it is a measure of the disorder of the system.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Put the three main states of matter in order from highest to lowest entropy.
back: The three main states of matter, in order from highest to lowest entropy, are: • Gas (highest entropy) • Liquid • Solid (lowest entropy)

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: True or False? Entropy and temperature remain constant during a change of state.
back: False. Temperature remains constant during a change of state, but entropy changes.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Does entropy increase or decrease during sublimation?
back: In sublimation, a solid becomes a gas so entropy increases.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Does entropy increase or decrease during freezing?
back: In freezing, a liquid becomes a solid so entropy decreases.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Other than changing state of matter, what are two situations in which entropy can increase?
back:
Entropy can also increase when
• A solid dissolves in a solvent
• A gas diffuses in a container

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Define a reversible process.
back: A reversible process is one where there is no overall change in entropy as the system and its surroundings are returned to their original states.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Define an irreversible process.
back: An irreversible process is one that results in an increase in entropy as the system and its surroundings cannot return to their original states.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: True or False? Processes occurring in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible.
back: True. Processes occurring in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible. The entropy of a real isolated system always increases.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Define an isolated system.
back: An isolated system is one in which neither matter nor energy can be transferred in or out.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: How does entropy change when heat is removed from a non-isolated system?
back: When heat is removed from a non-isolated system, its entropy can decrease locally.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: Why can the entropy of a non-isolated system decrease?
back: The entropy of a non-isolated system can decrease because this is compensated for by an equal, or greater increase in the entropy of the surroundings.

subtopicFull: B.4 Thermodynamics: First/second laws of thermodynamics, heat engines, entropy.
front: What is the net change in thermal energy transferred for a reversible process?
back:
For a reversible process:

\[
dS = \frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}
\]

so the reversible thermal energy transfer is:

\[
\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}} = T\,dS
\]

For an isothermal reversible process, this becomes:

\[
Q_{\mathrm{rev}} = T\Delta S
\]
