subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What are the two conditions for total internal reflection to occur?
back: The two conditions for total internal reflection to occur are: • the refractive index of medium 1 < refractive index of medium 2 () • angle of incidence > critical angle ()

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What is the equation for the critical angle, θc?
back: The equation for the critical angle, θc, is found using the equation: Where: • n2 = refractive index of medium 2 • n1 = refractive index of medium 1

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: How does the refractive index affect the speed of light in a medium?
back: The higher the refractive index of a material, the more optically dense it is, and the slower light will travel through it.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What is superposition?
back: Superposition is when two or more waves arrive at the same point and their amplitudes combine.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: Define the principle of superposition.
back: The principle of superposition states that when two or more waves overlap at a point, the displacement at that point is the sum of the displacements of the individual waves.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: True or False? Superposition only applies to transverse waves.
back: False. The principle of superposition applies to both transverse and longitudinal waves.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What does constructive interference mean?
back: Constructive interference occurs when two or more waves superimpose and have displacements in the same direction.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What is destructive interference?
back: Destructive interference occurs when two or more waves superimpose and have displacements in opposite directions.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: How do waves interfere constructively?
back: Waves interfere constructively when they are in phase and their displacements add together to form a larger displacement.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What happens to waves after they undergo superposition?
back: After waves undergo superposition, they continue to travel as normal.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: State the meaning of resultant displacement.
back: Resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements of individual waves when they overlap.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What must be constant for a clear interference pattern?
back: For a clear interference pattern, the waves must be of the same type, amplitude, frequency, and have a constant phase difference.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: Name the wave phenomenon that causes the amplitude of the resultant waves in the diagram to be the sum of the amplitudes of the two individual waves.
back: The amplitude of the resultant waves in the diagram is the sum of the amplitude of the two individual waves because the two waves are superposed.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: Determine the path difference between the waves coming from S 1 and S 2 in the diagram.
back: The path difference between the waves coming from S 1 and S 2 in the diagram is 2 λ.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What is double-source interference?
back: Double-source interference involves producing a diffraction and interference pattern using either two coherent wave sources or a single wave source passing through a double slit.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: State one example of a wave source that can cause double-source interference to be observed.
back: Double-source interference can be observed using the following wave sources: • A laser beam • Two speakers emitting coherent sound • Microwaves diffracted through two slits

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: Define interference.
back: Interference is the effect observed due to the superposition of two or more waves.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: When does constructive interference occur?
back: Constructive interference occurs when two waves meet in phase, resulting in the waves adding together.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: When does destructive interference occur?
back: Destructive interference occurs when two waves meet in antiphase, resulting in the waves cancelling each other out.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: True or False? Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
back: True. Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: Define path difference.
back: Path difference is the difference in the distance travelled by two waves from their sources to the point at which they meet.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What is the condition for constructive interference?
back: The condition for constructive interference is path difference = nλ, where n is an integer.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What is the condition for destructive interference?
back:
The condition for destructive interference is:

\[
\text{path difference} = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda
\]

where \(n\) is an integer.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: How is interference determined from a wavefront diagram?
back: On a wavefront diagram, interference is determined by counting the number of wavelengths to determine if constructive or destructive interference occurs at a point.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: State the features of a diffraction pattern that indicate a double-slit diffraction pattern.
back: The features of a diffraction pattern that indicate a double-slit diffraction pattern are: • each bright fringe is identical in width and intensity • the fringe spacing is equal

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: What is double-source interference?
back: Double-source interference involves producing a diffraction and interference pattern using either two coherent wave sources or a single wave source passing through a double slit.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: True or False? Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
back: True. Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: How is the nature of interference determined using a wavefront diagram?
back: The nature of interference is determined using a wavefront diagram by counting the number of wavelengths between the two wave sources to see if it is constructive or destructive at a point.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: Define monochromatic.
back: Monochromatic waves have the same wavelength, so for visible light, they are the same colour.

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: State the equipment required in Young's double slit experiment.
back: The equipment required in Young's double slit experiment is: a monochromatic light source; a single slit; a double slit; a screen

subtopicFull: C.3 Wave Phenomena: Diffraction, interference, single-slit, diffraction gratings.
front: State the type of diffraction observed by the screen shown in the diagram.
back: The type of diffraction observed on the screen shown in the diagram is double-slit diffraction.

subtopicFull: C.4 – Standing Waves And Resonance
front: Explain the equation: \(\lambda_n = \frac{2L}{n}\)
back:
This equation describes the activity of a radioactive sample. Meaning of each symbol:
\(A\) is the activity, the number of decays per second. Its unit is the becquerel, \(\mathrm{Bq}\).
\(\lambda\) is the decay constant. It represents the probability per unit time that one unstable nucleus will decay.
\(N\) is the number of undecayed radioactive nuclei remaining at time \(t\).
\(N_0\) is the original number of radioactive nuclei when \(t=0\). The equation says that activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei remaining. As time passes, \(N\) decreases exponentially, so the activity \(A\) also decreases exponentially.

back: A standing wave is produced by the superposition of two waves traveling in opposite directions with the same frequency.

back: False. Standing waves store energy. Progressive waves transfer energy.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is the main difference between progressive and standing waves?
back: The main difference is that progressive waves transfer energy, while standing waves store energy.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: Define a progressive wave.
back: A progressive wave is a wave that transfers energy from one place to another.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What conditions must be met for a standing wave to form?
back: For standing waves to form, the waves must have the same wavelength and a similar amplitude.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: True or False? The principle of superposition applies only to transverse waves.
back: False. The principle of superposition applies to all types of waves, including transverse, longitudinal, progressive, and stationary waves.

front: What is a node in a standing wave?

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.

back: An antinode is a location of maximum amplitude in a standing wave, where constructive interference occurs.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: True or False? Nodes are locations of maximum amplitude.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is the phase difference between two points with an odd number of nodes between them?
back: The phase difference between two points with an odd number of nodes between them is π (anti-phase).

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: Explain the difference between phase differences in standing and travelling waves.
back: The phase difference between two points on travelling waves can range from 0 to 2π, while in standing waves, they can only be 0 (in-phase) or π (anti-phase).

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.

front: True or False? A node is formed at the free end of a string or pipe.
back: False. At the free end of a string or pipe an antinode is formed (a location of maximum displacement).

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What does boundary condition mean in the context of standing waves?
back: Boundary condition refers to whether the ends of the medium (string or pipe) are fixed or free.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: How do boundary conditions affect the formation of standing waves?
back: Boundary conditions affect the formation of standing waves because they determine the positions of nodes and antinodes and the possible standing wave patterns.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: Define natural frequency.
back: Natural frequency is the specific frequency at which an integer number of half wavelengths fit on the length of the string or pipe.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is the effect of tension on the frequency of a vibrating string?
back: The frequency of a vibrating string increases with increasing tension.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: Which boundary conditions can exist for a pipe?
back: The boundary conditions that can exist for a pipe are: • closed at both ends • open at both ends • closed at one end and open at the other

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is the meaning of a fixed end in a standing wave?
back: A fixed end in a standing wave is a location of zero displacement, i.e., a node, where the reflected wave is in anti-phase with the incident wave.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.

front: Define a free oscillation.
back: A free oscillation is an oscillation where there are only internal forces (and no external forces) acting and no energy input.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is a forced oscillation?
back: A forced oscillation is an oscillation produced by a periodic external force.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: Define resonance.
back: Resonance is when the frequency of the applied force to an oscillating system is equal to its natural frequency, resulting in an oscillation at a maximum amplitude.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: Explain what happens to the amplitude of an object oscillating at resonance?
back: When oscillating at resonance the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system, causing the amplitude of the oscillations to reach its maximum.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: True or False? Free oscillations occur with no external forces acting on the system.

front: What is the driving frequency f of an oscillation?
back: The driving frequency f of an oscillation is the frequency of the periodic external force applied to an oscillating system.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is an example of resonance in everyday life?
back: An example of resonance in everyday life is pushing a child on a swing, where small pushes at the natural frequency increase the amplitude of the swing's motion.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is the effect of a periodic force on replacing the energy lost in damping?
back: The periodic force does work on resistive forces, sustaining oscillations by replacing the energy lost in damping.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: Define the damping of an oscillator.
back: The damping of an oscillator is the reduction in energy and amplitude of oscillations due to resistive forces on the oscillating system.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: When does light damping occur?
back: Light damping occurs when the amplitude of oscillations decreases exponentially with time.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is critical damping?
back: Critical damping is when an oscillator returns to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time without oscillating.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: What is heavy damping?
back: Heavy damping is when an oscillator takes time to return to its equilibrium position without oscillating.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: True or False? The frequency of damped oscillations changes as the amplitude decreases.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.
front: How does light damping affect a pendulum's motion?

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.

subtopicFull: C.4 Standing Waves and Resonance: Nodes, antinodes, standing waves on strings/in pipes.

subtopicFull: C.5 – Doppler Effect
front: Explain the equation: \(\frac{\Delta{f}}{f} = \frac{\Delta{\lambda}}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c}\)
back:
This is the approximate Doppler shift equation for electromagnetic waves when the source and observer are moving slowly compared with the speed of light. \[ \frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c} \] It says the fractional change in frequency or wavelength is approximately equal to the relative line-of-sight speed divided by the speed of light. Meaning of each symbol:
\(\Delta f\) = change in observed frequency
\(f\) = emitted frequency
\(\Delta \lambda\) = change in observed wavelength
\(\lambda\) = emitted wavelength
\(v\) = relative speed along the line of sight
\(c\) = speed of light For a source moving away, wavelength increases and frequency decreases. For a source moving towards the observer, wavelength decreases and frequency increases. The equation is usually used with magnitudes; the sign depends on whether the source is approaching or receding.

Doppler effect for electromagnetic waves
\(f\) frequency emitted by source
\(\lambda\) wavelength emitted by source
\(v\) velocity of source
\(c\) speed of light

subtopicFull: C.5 Doppler Effect: Sound and light Doppler effects.
front: Define the Doppler effect.
back:
The Doppler effect is the change in frequency due to the relative motion between a source of sound or light and an observer.

Useful formula — Doppler effect:
\[
f' = f\left(\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}\right)
\]

subtopicFull: C.5 Doppler Effect: Sound and light Doppler effects.
front: What happens to the frequency of a sound as the source moves away from a stationary observer?
back: The frequency of a sound appears to decrease as the source moves away from a stationary observer.

subtopicFull: C.5 Doppler Effect: Sound and light Doppler effects.
front: True or False? The Doppler effect only applies to sound waves.
back: False. The Doppler effect applies to both sound and electromagnetic waves. Useful formula — Doppler effect: \[ f' = f\left(\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}\right) \]

subtopicFull: C.5 Doppler Effect: Sound and light Doppler effects.
front: How does the wavelength of a sound change when the source moves towards a stationary observer?
back: The wavelength of a sound decreases when the source moves towards a stationary observer.

subtopicFull: C.5 Doppler Effect: Sound and light Doppler effects.
front: What happens in red shift?
back: In red shift, electromagnetic waves shift to the red end of the spectrum as they move away from the observer.

subtopicFull: C.5 Doppler Effect: Sound and light Doppler effects.
front: What happens in blue shift?
back: In blue shift, electromagnetic waves shift to the blue end of the spectrum as they move towards the stationary observer.

subtopicFull: C.5 Doppler Effect: Sound and light Doppler effects.
front: State the effect of the Doppler shift on light waves moving away from an observer.
back: The effect of the Doppler shift on light waves moving away from an observer is that the light waves are red-shifted, meaning their wavelength increases and frequency decreases.

back:
The gravitational force acting on an object in a gravitational field , per unit mass .

Useful formula — Gravitational field strength:
\[
g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}
\]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is Newton's law of gravitation?
back: Newton's law of gravitation states that the gravitational force between two point masses is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the gravitational force between two identical masses separated by a distance, r?
back: The gravitational force between the two identical masses is: Where: • G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10-11 N m2 kg–2) • M = magnitude of each mass, measured in kilograms (kg) • r = separation of the masses, measured in metres (m)

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The value of, G, (gravitational constant) is the same in all of space.
back: True. The value of, G, (gravitational constant) is the same in all of space.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The gravitational force between two masses can be attractive or repulsive.
back: False. The gravitational force between two masses is always attractive.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the relationship between gravitational force and distance?
back: The relationship between gravitational force and distance is an inverse square law. This means that when the distance between two point masses doubles, the gravitational force between them falls by .

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What assumptions are made about planets in Newton's law of gravitation?
back: The assumptions made about planets in Newton's law of gravitation are: • they are perfectly spherical • they are point masses (all the mass acts at their centres) • their separations are much greater than their radii

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Draw arrows to show the gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon.
back: The gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon: • is attractive (arrows point towards each other) • has the same magnitude on each object (arrows are the same size) • treats the objects as point masses (arrows begin from the centres)

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define gravitational field strength at a point.
back: The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a test mass at that point. Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What are the two equivalent units of gravitational field strength?
back: The two equivalent units of gravitational field strength are N kg-1 and m s-2. Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the significance of a test mass?
back: Test masses are used to define the strength of a field at a point and the direction a mass will movein the field. This is because gravitational field strength is a vector quantity.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? An object's mass changes depending on the strength of the gravitational field.
back: False. An object's mass remains the same at all points in space, but the force it experiences changes depending on the strength of the gravitational field.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Which two quantities does the strength of a gravitational field at the surface of a planet depend on?
back: The strength of a gravitational field at the surface of a planet depends on: • the radius of the planet • the mass of the planet

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the gravitational field strength due to a point mass of magnitude, M, at a distance, r?
back: The gravitational field strength due to a point mass is: Where: • G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10-11 N m2 kg–2) • M = magnitude of the point mass, measured in kilograms (kg) • r = distance from the mass to the point, measured in metres (m) Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The variation of gravitational field strength around a planet and a point mass are identical.
back: False. The variation of gravitational field strength around the outside of a planet and a point mass are identical. Inside the planet, the gravitational field strength decreases linearly from a maximum value (at the surface) to zero at the centre. Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: How is the resultant gravitational field due to multiple masses determined?
back: The resultant gravitational field due to multiple masses is determined by vector addition. This could be • using simple addition (if the point lies on a line joining the masses) • using Pythagoras (if the point makes a right-angled triangle with the masses)

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What do gravitational field lines represent?
back: Gravitational field lines represent • the strength of the gravitational field • the direction of the gravitational field

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is a uniform gravitational field?
back: A uniform gravitational field is one where the field strength is the same at all points.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Radial gravitational field lines always point towards the centre of mass of a body.
back: True. Radial gravitational field lines always point towards the centre of mass of a body.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Radial fields are considered uniform fields.
back: False. Radial fields are considered non-uniform fields.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the difference between radial and uniform gravitational fields?
back: The difference between radial and uniform gravitational fields is: • in a uniform gravitational field, field strength is the same at all points • in a radial gravitational field, field strength varies with distance from the centre

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the relationship between gravitational field strength and line density?
back: The density of field lines represents the strength of a gravitational field • the closer together the field lines, the stronger the field • the further apart the field lines, the weaker the field Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define gravitational potential at a point.
back: The gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to a defined point.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Gravitational potential is a vector quantity.
back: False. Gravitational potential is a scalar quantity.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the unit of gravitational potential?
back:
Kepler's third law states that, for objects orbiting the same central body:

\[
T^2 \propto r^3
\]

or equivalently:

\[
\frac{T^2}{r^3} = \text{constant}
\]

where \(T\) is the orbital period and \(r\) is the orbital radius.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Gravitational potential is always positive.
back: False. Gravitational potential is always negative.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the gravitational potential due to a point mass of magnitude, M, at a distance, r?
back: The gravitational potential due to a point mass is: Where: • G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10-11 N m2 kg–2) • M = mass producing the gravitational field, measured in kilograms (kg) • r = distance from the centre of the mass to the point mass, measured in metres (m)

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Gravitational potential increases with distance from a planet.
back: True. Gravitational potential increases (becomes less negative) with distance from a planet.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What happens to gravitational potential as r approaches infinity?
back: As r approaches infinity, gravitational potential approaches zero.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The combined gravitational potential at a point due to multiple point masses is determined by vector addition.
back: False. The combined gravitational potential at a point due to multiple point masses is determined by adding together the potential due to each mass.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define gravitational potential energy of a system.
back: The gravitational potential energy of a system is the work done when bringing all the masses in a systemto their positions from infinity. Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define gravitational potential energy of a point mass.
back: The gravitational potential energy of a point mass is the work done in bringing the point mass from infinity to a point. Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface?
back: The gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface is: Where: • m = mass, measured in kilograms (kg) • g = gravitational field strength (9.8 N kg–1) • Δh = change in height above surface, measured in metres (m) Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The gravitational potential energy on the surface of a planet is taken to be zero.
back: True. The gravitational potential energy on the surface of a planet is taken to be zero. Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? An input of work is required to move a mass against a gravitational field.
back: True. An input of work is required to move a mass against a gravitational field.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the work done in moving a mass, m, in a gravitational field?
back: The work done in moving a mass, m, in a gravitational field is: Where: • W = work done in moving mass, measured in joules (J) • m = magnitude of mass moving in the field, measured in kilograms (kg) • ΔV = potential difference between two points, measured in joules per kilogram (J kg−1) Useful formula — Work done: \[ W = Fs\cos\theta \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define gravitational potential difference.
back: Gravitational potential difference is the difference in gravitational potential between two points. It is equal to the work done when a mass of 1 kg is moved between the points. Useful formula — Potential difference: \[ V = \frac{W}{q} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the potential difference due to a point mass M when a mass is moved from a distance r2 to r1?
back: The potential difference due to a point mass is: Where: • G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10-11 N m2 kg–2) • M = magnitude of mass producing the potential, measured in kilograms (kg) • r2 = initial distance from charge M, measured in metres (m) • r1 = final distance from charge M, measured in metres (m) Useful formula — Potential difference: \[ V = \frac{W}{q} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: State the equation for the gravitational potential energy of two point masses.
back: The gravitational potential energy of two point masses is: Where: • G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10-11 N m2 kg–2) • M = larger mass producing the field, measured in kilograms (kg) • m = mass moving within the field of M, measured in kilograms (kg) • r = distance between the centres of the masses, measured in metres (m) Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What happens to the gravitational potential energy as a satellite moves away from a planet?
back: The gravitational potential energy increases as a satellite moves away from a planet. When a small mass moves away from a large mass, the gravitational potential energy always increases. Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What happens to the gravitational potential energy as a satellite moves towards a planet?
back: The gravitational potential energy decreases as a satellite moves towards a planet. When a small mass moves towards a large mass, the gravitational potential energy always decreases. Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What does the area under a force-distance graph represent?
back: The area under a force-distance graph represents the change in gravitational potential energy or the work done in moving the mass from one point to another.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: When a small mass m moves away from a larger mass M, what is the change in gravitational potential energy?
back: The change in gravitational potential energy (or work done) is: Where: • G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10-11 N m2 kg–2) • M = larger mass producing the field, measured in metres (kg) • m = mass moving within the field of M, measured in kilograms (kg) • r1 = initial separation between masses, measured in metres (m) • r2 = final separation between masses, measured in metres (m) Useful formula — Gravitational potential energy: \[ \Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define the potential gradient of a gravitational field.
back: Gravitational gradient is the rate of change of gravitational potential with respect to displacement in the direction of the field.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What does the negative sign indicate in the potential gradient equation?
back: In the potential gradient equation the negative sign indicates that the direction of the field strength gopposes the direction of increasing potential.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What does the gradient of a V − r graph represent?
back: The gradient of a potential-distance (V − r) graph represents the gravitational field strength at that point.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What does the area under a g − r graph represent?
back: The area under a field-distance (g − r) graph represents the potential difference between the two points.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The V − r graph follows a 1/r relation.
back: False. The potential-distance (V − r) graph follows a −1/r relation. All values of gravitational potential are negative.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The curve of a g − r graph is steeper than its corresponding V − r graph.
back: True. The curve of a g − r graph is steeper than its corresponding V − r graph. This is because g − r graphs follow a 1/r2 relation whereas V − r graphs follow a −1/r relation.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to gravitational field lines.
back: True. Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to gravitational field lines.

front: State Kepler's first law.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: At what point in a comet's orbit does it travel fastest?
back: Comets travel fastest when they are at the closest point to the Sun in their elliptical orbit.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: At what point in a comet's orbit does it travel slowest?
back: Comets travel slowest when they are at the furthest point from the Sun in their elliptical orbit.

front: True or False? A graph of log T against log r for the planets in the Solar System is a straight line.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define escape speed.
back: Escape speed is the minimum speed that will allow an object to escape a gravitational field with no further energy input.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Escape speed depends on the mass of the escaping object.
back: False. Escape speed is the same for all masses in the same gravitational field.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: State the equation for escape speed.
back:
The escape speed from a spherical body is:

\[
v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}
\]

where \(G\) is the gravitational constant, \(M\) is the mass of the body being escaped from, and \(r\) is the distance from its centre of mass.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Escape speed is the speed needed to escape a planet's surface.
back: False. Escape speed is the speed needed to escape a planet's gravitational field altogether.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: How does the mass of the planet affect escape speed?
back: The relationship between escape speed and the mass of a planet is: Therefore, the greater the mass of a planet, the greater the escape speed.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: How does escape speed vary with distance from the centre of a planet?
back: The relationship between escape speed and distance from the centre of a planet is: Therefore, escape speed decreases with distance from the centre of a planet.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Why don't satellites being launched into an orbit around the Earth need to achieve escape speed?
back: Satellites launched from Earth's surface do not need to achieve escape velocity to reach orbit because • the escape speed equation assumes the mass starts with zero kinetic energy, but the thrust from fuel provides a continuous source of energy • less energy is needed to achieve orbit than to escape from Earth's gravitational field

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define orbital speed.
back: Orbital speed is the minimum speed required for an object to maintain a circular orbit.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? All satellites at the same orbital radius have the same orbital speed, regardless of their mass.
back: True. All satellites at the same orbital radius have the same orbital speed, regardless of their mass.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? As a satellite's orbital radius decreases, its kinetic energy increases.
back: True. As a satellite's orbital radius decreases, its kinetic energy increases.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? As a satellite's orbital radius increases, its potential energy decreases.
back: False. As a satellite's orbital radius increases, its potential energy increases.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Satellites in low orbits are not affected by air resistance.
back: False. Satellites in low orbits (<600 km) can be affected by air resistance.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the effect of drag on a satellite's orbit over time?
back: The effect of drag on a satellite's orbit over time is a decrease in height and an increase in orbital speed.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What factors must be considered to provide enough energy to a satellite to put it into orbit?
back: To provide enough energy to a satellite to put it into orbit, the factors that must be considered are: • the increase in gravitational potential energy between the Earth's surface and the height of the satellite's orbit • the required kinetic energy for the correct orbital speed of the satellite (to maintain a circular orbit) • the satellite must overcome frictional forces • additional energy must be allowed for thermal energy dissipation

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What happens to the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit as its orbit becomes lower due to drag?
back: As a satellite's orbit becomes lower due to drag, its orbital speed increases. This is because some of its potential energy has been transferred to kinetic energy.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What happens to the total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit as its orbit becomes lower due to drag?
back: As a satellite's orbit becomes lower due to drag, its total energy decreases. This is because some energy has been dissipated.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is Newton's law of gravitation?
back: Newton's law of gravitation states that the gravitational force between two point masses is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the gravitational force between two identical masses separated by a distance, r?
back: The gravitational force between the two identical masses is: Where: • G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10−11 N m2 kg−2) • M = magnitude of each mass, measured in kilograms (kg) • r = separation of the masses, measured in metres (m)

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The value of, G, (gravitational constant) is the same in all of space.
back: True. The value of, G, (gravitational constant) is the same in all of space.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The gravitational force between two masses can be attractive or repulsive.
back: False. The gravitational force between two masses is always attractive.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the relationship between gravitational force and distance?
back: The relationship between gravitational force and distance is an inverse square law. This means that when the distance between two point masses doubles, the gravitational force between them falls by ¼.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What assumptions are made about planets in Newton's law of gravitation?
back: The assumptions made about planets in Newton's law of gravitation are: • they are perfectly spherical • they are point masses (all the mass acts at their centres) • their separations are much greater than their radii

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Draw arrows to show the gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon.
back: The gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon: • is attractive (arrows point towards each other) • has the same magnitude on each object (arrows are the same size) • treats the objects as point masses (arrows begin from the centres)

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Define gravitational field strength at a point.
back: The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a test mass at that point. Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What are the two equivalent units of gravitational field strength?
back: The two equivalent units of gravitational field strength are N kg−1 and m s−2. Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the significance of a test mass?
back: Test masses are used to define the strength of a field at a point and the direction a mass will move in the field. This is because gravitational field strength is a vector quantity.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? An object's mass changes depending on the strength of the gravitational field.
back: False. An object's mass remains the same at all points in space, but the force it experiences changes depending on the strength of the gravitational field.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: Which two quantities does the strength of a gravitational field at the surface of a planet depend on?
back: The strength of a gravitational field at the surface of a planet depends on: • the radius of the planet • the mass of the planet

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the gravitational field strength due to a point mass of magnitude, M, at a distance, r?
back: The gravitational field strength due to a point mass is: Where: G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10−11 N m2 kg−2); M = magnitude of the point mass, measured in kilograms (kg); r = distance from the mass to the point, measured in metres (m) Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? The variation of gravitational field strength around a planet and a point mass are identical.
back: False. The variation of gravitational field strength around the outside of a planet and a point mass are identical. Inside the planet, the gravitational field strength decreases linearly from a maximum value (at the surface) to zero at the centre. Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: How is the resultant gravitational field due to multiple masses determined?
back: The resultant gravitational field due to multiple masses is determined by vector addition. This could be using simple addition (if the point lies on a line joining the masses); using Pythagoras (if the point makes a right-angled triangle with the masses)

front: What do gravitational field lines represent?
back: Gravitational field lines represent • the strength of the gravitational field • the direction of the gravitational field

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is a uniform gravitational field?
back: A uniform gravitational field is one where the field strength is the same at all points.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Radial gravitational field lines always point towards the centre of mass of a body.
back: True. Radial gravitational field lines always point towards the centre of mass of a body.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: True or False? Radial fields are considered uniform fields.
back: False. Radial fields are considered non-uniform fields.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: What is the difference between radial and uniform gravitational fields?
back: The difference between radial and uniform gravitational fields is: • in a uniform gravitational field, field strength is the same at all points • in a radial gravitational field, field strength varies with distance from the centre

front: What is the relationship between gravitational field strength and line density?
back: The density of field lines represents the strength of a gravitational field • the closer together the field lines, the stronger the field • the further apart the field lines, the weaker the field Useful formula — Gravitational field strength: \[ g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: State Kepler's first law.
back: Kepler's first law states that the orbit of a planet is an ellipse, with the Sun at one of the two foci.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: State Kepler's second law.
back: Kepler's second law states that a line segment joining the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals.

subtopicFull: D.1 Gravitational Fields: Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational potential.
front: State Kepler's third law.
back:
Kepler's third law states that, for planets or satellites orbiting the same central body:

\[
T^2 \propto r^3
\]

or equivalently:

\[
\frac{T^2}{r^3} = \text{constant}
\]

For two objects orbiting the same central body:

\[
\frac{T_1^2}{r_1^3} = \frac{T_2^2}{r_2^3}
\]

where \(T\) is the orbital period and \(r\) is the orbital radius.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Define 1 coulomb (C).
back: 1 coulomb is the charge carried by an electric current of one ampere in one second. Useful formula — Coulomb’s law: \[ F = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? Charge is a vector quantity.
back: False. Charge is a scalar quantity. It has magnitude only, not direction.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How is this carbon atom electrically neutral?
back: The carbon atom contains: • 6 positive protons • 6 negative electrons • 6 neutral neutrons The amount of positive and negative charge is equal, so the carbon atom iselectrically neutral.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How is charge quantised?
back: Charge is quantised because any quantity of charge will always equal a whole number of protons or electrons, which have a charge equal to ±1.60 × 10−19 C.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Is the electric force between two charges of the same type attractive or repulsive?
back: The electric force on two charges of the same type is repulsive (directed away from each other).

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Is the electric force between two opposite charges attractive or repulsive?
back: The electric force on two opposite charges is attractive (directed towards each other).

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the law of conservation of charge?
back: The law of conservation of charge states that the total charge in an isolated system remains constant.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? When two charged spheres come into contact, the charges are shared between them until they are evenly distributed.
back: True. When two charged spheres come into contact, the charges are shared between them until they are evenly distributed. As a result, both spheres will have an equal charge.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the final charge on two spheres of initial charge +1 C and +9 C when brought into contact?
back: According to the law of conservation of charge, the final charge on each sphere is equal to the average of the two charges

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the final charge on two spheres of initial charge +4 C and -4 C when brought into contact?
back: According to the law of conservation of charge, the final charge on each sphere is equal to the average of the two charges 0 C •

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What does Millikan's oil drop experiment provide evidence for?
back: Millikan's oil drop experiment provides evidence for the quantisation of charge.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is meant by the term fundamental charge?
back: The fundamental charge (or elementary charge) is the charge of a single proton (+1.60 × 10−19 C) or electron (-1.60 × 10−19 C).

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: In Millikan's experiment, why are oil drops used instead of water?
back: In Millikan's experiment, oil drops are used as they do not evaporate quickly like water. This allows the mass of the drops to remain constant throughout the experiment.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: In Millikan's experiment, how do the oil drops become charged?
back: In Millikan's experiment, the oil drops can become charged by • friction (using a spray nozzle) • ionisation (using X-rays)

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: In Millikan's experiment, what happens to the oil drops in the absence of an electric field?
back: In Millikan's experiment, when no electric field is applied, the oil drops fall under gravity until they reach a terminal velocity.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the role of the uniform electric field in Millikan's experiment?
back: In Millikan's experiment, the uniform electric field provides an electric force which is equal and opposite to the gravitational force on an oil drop. The resultant force will then be zero and the drop will become stationary.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: In Millikan's experiment, what quantities are needed to calculate the charge of an oil drop?
back: In Millikan's experiment, the charge of an oil drop is calculated by equating the gravitational and electric forces Therefore, the quantities needed to calculate the charge, q, are: • the mass of the drop, m • the potential difference between the metal plates, V • the distance between the metal plates, d

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What was the conclusion of Millikan's experiment?
back: The conclusion of Millikan's experiment was: • the charges of all drops were found to be multiples of the same number (-1.60 × 10−19 C) • therefore, electric charge must be a quantised quantity

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is charging by friction?
back: Charging by friction is the transfer of charge (electrons) when two insulating substances move past one another. One substance gains an excess of positive charge and the other gains an excess of negative charge.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is charging by contact?
back: Charging by contact is the transfer of charge (electrons) between two substances when there is physical contact between them. The excess, or deficit, of electrons, is shared between the two substances.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is charging by induction?
back: Charging by induction is the separation of charge caused by the influence of a nearby charged object without any physical contact. The charged object causes electrons near the surface of the uncharged substance to be either repelled or attracted.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Describe the movement of electrons when an uncharged acetate rod is rubbed with an uncharged cloth.
back: When an uncharged acetate rod is rubbed with an uncharged cloth: • electrons are transferred from the acetate rod to the cloth by friction • the cloth becomes negatively charged because it gains electrons • the acetate rod becomes positively charged because it loses electrons

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? Earthing a charged body causes it to discharge until its potential drops to half its initial value.
back: False. Earthing a charged body causes it to discharge until it has a potential of 0 V.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How can a metal sphere become charged by induction?
back: A metal sphere can become charged by induction by • bringing a charged rod near the sphere without touching it (this separates the charges) • earthing the sphere (this allows electrons to flow to or from the sphere) • removing the earth connection and the rod (this leaves an excess charge)

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? A metal sphere can become positively charged by induction by using a positively charged rod.
back: False. A metal sphere can become positively charged by induction by using a negatively charged rod. When inducing a charge on a metal sphere, its final charge will always be opposite to the rod.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How can a metal sphere become charged by contact?
back: A metal sphere can become charged by contact by • bringing a charged rod into contact with the sphere (this allows electrons to flow to or from the sphere) • removing the rod (this leaves an excess charge)

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How can sparks occur when refuelling an aircraft?
back: Sparks can occur when • there is a large build-up of charge on the aircraft • the potential difference becomes large enough for current to travel through the air

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How can the risk of sparks be reduced when refuelling an aircraft?
back: When refuelling an aircraft, the risk of sparking can be reduced by earthing the aircraft and fuel tank to carry excess charge away.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is Coulomb's law?
back: Coulomb's lawstates that the electric force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. Useful formula — Coulomb’s law: \[ F = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the electric force between two identical charges of magnitude, q, separated by a distance, r?
back: The electric force between the two identical charges is: Where: • k = Coulomb constant (8.99 × 109 N m2 C–2) • q = magnitude of the charges (C) • r = separation of the charges (m)

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How is Coulomb's law analogous to Newton's law of gravitation?
back: Coulomb's law: Newton's law of gravitation: Both electric force and gravitational force follow an inverse square law with distance. Useful formula — Coulomb’s law: \[ F = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Is the electric force between two opposite charges positive or negative?
back: The electric force between two opposite charges is negative. A negative force means the force is attractive.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Is the electric force between two similar charges positive or negative?
back: The electric force between two similar charges is positive. A positive force means the force is repulsive.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? Coulomb's law can be applied to any charged object regardless of shape or size.
back: False. Coulomb's law can only be applied to charged spheres. Useful formula — Coulomb’s law: \[ F = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? The value of, k, (Coulomb constant) is the same in all materials.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the permittivity of a medium?
back: The permittivity of a medium represents the medium's ability to transfer an electric field and force between charges in it.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How is the permittivity of a medium related to the permittivity of free space?
back: The permittivity of a medium is related to the permittivity of free space by: Where: • εr = relative permittivity • ε = permittivity of a medium • ε0 = permittivity of free space

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? All materials have a higher relative permittivity than air.
back: True. All materials have a higher relative permittivity than air. • Relative permittivity of air: • Relative permittivity of other materials:

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Define electric field strength at a point.
back: The electric field strength at a point is the force per unit charge experienced by a small positive test charge placed at that point. Useful formula — Electric field strength: \[ E = \frac{F}{q} = \frac{kQ}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What are the two equivalent units of electric field strength?
back: The two equivalent units of electric field strength are N C-1 and V m-1. Useful formula — Electric field strength: \[ E = \frac{F}{q} = \frac{kQ}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the significance of a test charge?
back: Test charges are used to define the strength of a field at a point and the direction a charge will movein the field. This is because electric field strength is a vector quantity.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How is the direction of an electric field defined?
back: The direction of an electric field is defined by the direction of the force that acts on a positive test charge, such that • the force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field • the force on a negative charge is in the opposite direction

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What is the electric field strength due to a point charge of magnitude, q, at a distance, r?
back: The electric field strength due to a point charge is: Where: • k = Coulomb constant (8.99 × 109 N m2 C–2) • q = magnitude of the charge (C) • r = distance from the charge to the point (m) Useful formula — Electric field strength: \[ E = \frac{F}{q} = \frac{kQ}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: True or False? The variation of electric field strength around a charged sphere and a point charge are identical.
back: False. The variation of electric field strength around the outside of a charged sphere and a point charge are identical. Inside the charged sphere, the electric field strength is zero. Useful formula — Electric field strength: \[ E = \frac{F}{q} = \frac{kQ}{r^2} \]

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How is the resultant electric field due to multiple charges determined?
back: The resultant electric field due to multiple charges is determined by vector addition. This could be • using simple addition (if the point lies on a line joining the charges) • using Pythagoras (if the point makes a right-angled triangle with the charges)

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: How is a uniform electric field set up?
back: A uniform electric field can be set up between two parallel metal plates by connecting them to the terminals of a power supply.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: Which two quantities does the strength of an electric field between two parallel plates depend on?
back: The strength of an electric field between two parallel plates is: Where: • V = potential difference between the plates (V) • d = separation of the plates (m)

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: An electron is placed in the uniform electric field shown in the diagram. In which direction will it move?
back: The electron will move to the left towards the positively charged plate.

subtopicFull: D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields: Coulomb’s law, field patterns.
front: What do electric field lines represent?
back: Electric field lines represent • the strength of the electric field • the direction of the electric field
