subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What is nuclear fusion?
back: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two smaller nuclei to form one larger nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy in the process.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Where does nuclear fusion take place in stars?
back: Nuclear fusion takes place in the centres (cores) of stars.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Why do nuclei require very high kinetic energies in order to fuse?
back: Nuclei require very high kinetic energies to fuse to • overcome the repulsive coulomb forces between protons • get close enough for the strong nuclear force to act

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Write a nuclear equation for the fusion of two hydrogen-1 nuclei into a hydrogen-2 nucleus.
back: The nuclear equation is: = hydrogen-1 nucleus, or a proton. = hydrogen-2 nucleus. = a positron; νe = an electron neutrino.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: In what form is energy released from nuclear fusion reactions?
back: In fusion reactions, energy is released in the form of kinetic energy of the nuclei produced as well as gamma rays and neutrinos.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? In a nuclear fusion reaction, the mass of the fused nucleus is the same as the mass of the two nuclei that fused together.
back: False. In a nuclear fusion reaction, the mass of the fused nucleus is less than the mass of the two nuclei that fused together. The remaining mass has been converted to energy.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front:
Calculate the energy released each time deuterium and tritium fuse into helium:
Deuterium (hydrogen-2) has a binding energy of 1.11 MeV per nucleon, tritium (hydrogen-3) has a binding energy of 2.83 MeV per nucleon, and helium-4 has a binding energy of 7.07 MeV per nucleon.
back: The energy released per fusion is about 17.6 MeV. calculate the binding energy before the reaction = (1.11 × 2) + (2.83 × 3); calculate the binding energy after the reaction = (7.07 × 4); determine the difference in binding energy = (7.07 × 4) - (1.11 × 2) - (2.83 × 3) = 17.57 MeV Useful formula — Binding energy: \[ E_b = \Delta m c^2 \]

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? Fission reactions release more energy per kg than fusion reactions.
back: False. Fusion reactions release much more energy per kg than fission.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What two conditions are required for nuclear fusion to occur?
back: The two conditions required for nuclear fusion to occur are: • High temperature • High pressure or density

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What is radiation pressure?
back: Radiation pressure is a pressure that arises due to the transfer of momentum from photons to the surrounding matter.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: How do main sequence stars remain in equilibrium?
back: Main sequence stars remain in equilibrium because fusion reactions generate radiation pressure which acts outwards and balances the inwards-acting gravitational force.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: When does a protostar become a main sequence star?
back: A protostar becomes a main sequence star when nuclear fusion reactions are initiated in its core and the inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from the fusion reactions.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? All stars form from a cloud of dust and gas which becomes a protostar and then a main sequence star.
back: True. All stars follow the same initial stages in their life cycle: • Nebula (cloud of dust and gas) • Protostar • Main sequence star The stages that follow depend on the mass of the main sequence star that forms.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Name the stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star similar to the Sun.
back: The stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star similar to the Sun are: Nebula (cloud of dust and gas); Protostar; Main sequence star; Red giant; Planetary nebula; White dwarf

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: When does a main sequence star turn into a red giant?
back: A main sequence star turns into a red giant when hydrogen in the star's core begins to run out and the star begins to fuse helium into heavier elements.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? A high-mass star will eventually explode as a supernova and become a white dwarf.
back: False. A high mass star will eventually explode as a supernova and become a neutron star or a black hole.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Name the stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star with a mass larger than the Sun.
back: The stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star with a mass larger than the Sun are: Nebula (cloud of dust and gas); Protostar; Main sequence; Red supergiant; Supernova; Black hole, or neutron star

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What is a supernova?
back: A supernova is a large exploding star.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Under what conditions does a supernova occur?
back: A supernova occurs when a star much more massive than the Sun reaches the end of its red supergiant stage. It collapses, becomes very unstable and explodes.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What determines whether the remnant core of a massive star becomes a neutron star or a black hole?
back: The mass of the remnant core determines whether a massive star becomes a neutron star or a black hole.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? High-mass stars have significantly longer lifetimes than low-mass stars.
back: False. High-mass stars have significantly shorter lifetimes than low-mass stars. The greater the mass of a star, the higher its temperature, therefore, the greater the rate of fusion and the quicker the fuel is depleted in its core.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What is a Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram?
back: The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram is a plot of a star's luminosity on the y-axis and its surface temperature on the x-axis.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Which star on the H-R diagram has the highest surface temperature, A, B, C or D?
back: The star with the highest surface temperature is star B. The hottest stars are located towards the left side of the H-R diagram.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Which star on the H-R diagram has the lowest surface temperature, A, B, C or D?
back: The star with the coolest surface temperature is star D. The coolest stars are located towards the right side of the H-R diagram.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Which star on the H-R diagram is the brightest, A, B, C or D?
back: The brightest star is star A. The brightest stars are found near the top of the H-R diagram.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Which star on the H-R diagram is most similar to the Sun, A, B, C or D?
back: The most similar star to the Sun is star C. The luminosity scale is given in solar units, where the luminosity of the Sun = 1

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Where is the main sequence located on the H-R diagram?
back: On the H-R diagram, main sequence stars are stars found in a band from the top left to the bottom right.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Where are white dwarfs located on the H-R diagram?
back: On the H-R diagram, white dwarfs are located below the main sequence and slightly to the left.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Where are red giants located on the H-R diagram?
back: On the H-R diagram, red giants are located above the main sequence and slightly to the right.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What type of stars are the hottest and dimmest on the H-R diagram?
back: The hottest and dimmest stars on the H-R diagram are white dwarfs.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What type of stars are the coolest and brightest on the H-R diagram?
back: The coolest and brightest stars on the H-R diagram are red supergiants.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What are the three types of light spectra?
back: The three types of light spectra are: • continuous spectra • emission spectra • absorption spectra

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? Absorption spectra are observed when white light passes through a hot, low-pressure gas.
back: False. Absorption spectra are observed when white light passes through a cool, low-pressure gas.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? Continuous spectra are produced by hot, dense sources.
back: True. Continuous spectra are produced from hot, dense sources, such as the cores of stars.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Why do stars emit absorption spectra?
back: Stars emit absorption spectra because: • the hot, dense core produces a continuous spectrum • the cool, low-density gas in the outer layers absorbs photons • the resulting spectrum is a set of dark lines on a coloured background

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: How can the chemical composition of a star be determined?
back: The chemical composition of a star can be determined by analyzing its absorption spectrum and identifying elements by their unique pattern of spectral lines.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Define 1 astronomical unit (AU).
back: One astronomical unit (AU) is the mean distance between the centre of the Earth and the centre of the Sun. 1 AU is equal to approximately 1.5 × 1011 m.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Define 1 light-year (ly).
back: One light-year is the distance travelled by light in one year. 1 ly is equal to approximately 9.5 × 1015 m.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: Define 1 parsec (pc).
back: One parsec is a unit of distance that gives a parallax angle of 1 second of an arc. 1 pc is equal to approximately 3.1 × 1016 m.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: What is stellar parallax?
back: Stellar parallax is the displacement in the apparent position of a nearby star against a background of distant stars when viewed from different positions of the Earth during its orbit around the Sun.

subtopicFull: E.5 Fusion and Stars: Stellar energy, luminosity, Wien’s law, Stefan-Boltzmann law.
front: True or False? Stellar parallax is accurate for measuring distances up to about 100 light-years.
back: False. Stellar parallax is accurate for measuring distances up to about 100 parsecs.

front: What information is needed to calculate the radius of a star using the Stefan-Boltzmann law?
back: To calculate the radius of a star using the Stefan-Boltzmann law: • surface temperature can be calculated using Wien’s displacement law • luminosity can be calculated using the inverse square law of flux equation Useful formula — Stefan–Boltzmann law: \[ P = \sigma A T^4 \]
